body.text: Kaurna artists reframe community through tintype photography
When Joan Lamont looks at the greyscale portraits of her Kaurna mob placed side by side, she sees the eyes of her ancestors looking back at her.
"How they look … is like looking back and seeing the old people come back to them," the Kaurna Narungga elder said.
The tintype portraits of her living community members have just finished developing and are drying out on a table next to a makeshift darkroom in a bathroom.
The 83-year-old has just sat for her own tintype portrait taken by Kaurna artists James Tylor and Damien Shen in the Art Gallery of South Australia's courtyard.
Tylor and Shen spent a week in October with a vintage Linhof camera capturing their community in the analogue format.

The photo shoot is part of an international project the Critical Indigenous Photo Exchange (CIPX), started by Navajo man Will Wilson when he began using the tintype photography — popular during colonial era — to take striking portraits of his contemporary community.
Tylor and Shen's photos taken in this shoot in Adelaide will be blown up and displayed on the walls of SA's art gallery in coming weeks.
"It makes me very emotional that we will live on, you know,"
"We may die off, I don't think so, but we could.
"But we'll be up there, looking down on everyone and everyone will know who we are."
A camera with a colonial past
The tintype camera was developed in the mid-19th century and uses the wet plate photography process.
Travellers and anthropologists across the world often towed around a tintype camera, and photographed many First Nations people as subjects.
In South Australia, Damien Shen has photos taken of his own great grandparents in 1939 at Raukkan (Point McLeay Mission) by anthropologist Norman Tindale.

"When I look at that and consider what was happening in that time, it's hard to know what type of consent was given by my family in terms of being captured in the way they were, if they really understood what was happening,"
"I try to interrogate that and retell that through some of my practice now."
Shen has seen the way Aboriginal people were portrayed in historical photography by settlers in colonial Australia.

"What I have looked at is the way there's like an anthropological or an ethnographic gaze on Aboriginal people since like the 19th century and how those images have been captured, essentially portraying Aboriginal people as like the 'other'," he said.

"Looking into that aspect of it has always fascinated me and I guess that's a little bit evident in some of the practice of mine over the years, and how I've then used photography to sort of retell that story."
Tylor and Shen's subjects for the project get to choose what they wear and how they are portrayed.

Once the physical tin has been digitally captured, the Kaurna community member keeps the original plate and choose exactly how the digital photograph can be stored and shared, including if it will be part of Tylor and Shen's exhibition.
The week-long photo shoot had a daily run sheet of prominent members in the Kaurna community, of the Adelaide Plains in South Australia, who took turns in front of the vintage lens.

The wet plate photography process involves brushing a formula called collodion on black metal plate, placing it in a tank of silver nitrate for a few minutes before loading it in a light-safe camera cartridge and then into a tintype camera itself.

Once the photo is taken, the cartridge is taken to a dark room, developer solution is poured over for 10 to 15 seconds before it is submerged in a stop bath of water for several minutes and eventually placed into a fixing solution.
For Shen, the shoot is not just about capturing portraits, but also what happens on the sidelines.
"We're talking about family while we're doing it and other members of community are coming in and sitting down and chatting,"
he said.
"It's been quite a communal and a beautiful process."
With an exposure time of 7 seconds and many variables in the tintype process, reshoots are often required and there may be several sheets of tin used before the perfect portrait is taken.
While the format may be a fickle one, the final products capture striking imagery of the Kaurna community in a way that not only refers back to a previous era, but reshapes it in a modern context.
Ms Lamont said she felt pride and joy in taking part in the project, which will be exhibited at the art gallery until the end of March.
"It's a real connection of us coming together and doing this wonderful, beautiful thing that will have us there looking at people," she said.
"It is timeless, beautiful; and we are working together as one to show who we are.
"We're the oldest people in the universe and we should be more appreciated as survivors."
